When I joined the company, the legal team had a backlog of almost two hundred contracts, and the sales team called us the bottleneck. So we changed three things. First, we wrote a playbook: one page for each type of contract, with our standard position on every clause. Second, we had a tool do the first pass on every NDA. It compares the draft with the playbook and highlights anything unusual. Third, and this is the part people forget, we had a lawyer read every redline before it went out. Our turnaround time for an NDA went from five days to one. But I always tell new people the same thing: the tool is fast, but it is not responsible. If you sign it, you have read it. Last month, I got the vendor to show us exactly where our documents are stored, and I am very glad I asked.

Two years ago, we had an AI tool review a supply agreement with a new partner in Ohio. The report was clean: no red flags, nothing outside the playbook. I was about to sign it. Then a junior associate, who was in her second week, asked if she could read it once more. She found the problem on page fourteen. The partner had changed the definition of losses, and with that one change, our liability cap almost disappeared. The tool had compared the clauses, but it had not read the definitions carefully. I took two lessons from that day. First, I had our checklist updated, so that a person now reads every definition in full. Second, I never again let a clean report replace a careful reading. A clean report tells you what the tool found. It does not tell you what it missed.

First, a US partner sends Pedro's team an NDA and asks for comments by Friday. Then Pedro has the tool do a first pass and flag the unusual clauses. Next, he reads the redline himself and finds a clause on data that the tool did not flag. After that, he gets the partner to explain where the shared data will be stored. Finally, he signs off on the NDA and has the dates added to the contract tracker.
